en: For the forty companions, forty tombs
He built in wondrous fashion.
There were ninety trading Sarts,
With Kyzyl Sart as caravan leader.
Making friends with Kyzyl Sart,
He summoned the Sarts' craftsmen.
He had them knead and tread the clay,
And cattle hair mixed with goat hair
He had scattered into the clay.
Whether it stood crooked or straight,
He had Kyzyl Sart inspect it.
For the forty companions, forty tombs
He had Surkyzyl slaughtered.
“May all the people dwelling here
Butt one another like rams,” he said.
That place where the tombs stood
He had named “Kochkor” and “Chyybyt.”
Having buried the forty companions, Semetey
Received Khan Bakai's blessing.
Thus that place
Came to be called Kochkor.
After slaughtering the forty companions,
After slaughtering them and finding relief,
He returned to Talas.
Semetey had no regret,
And became a sultan in Talas.
His name was heard in Alai,
His spiritual might spread far and wide.
He stood firm by his word,
A noble scion as strong as iron,
Maintaining a royal court, a khan,
A man born of saints.
Word was sent to the people.
They set a golden crown upon him,
And seated him upon a golden throne.
Over the Argyn and the Kyrgyz
They gave him unshaken rule,
And raised him as khan.
His father, gray-maned Manas—
Semetey was born surpassing him,
And now became a sultan.
Of the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
He joined what had been torn,
And gathered what had been scattered.
All his twelve bodily members grew complete.
Manas, who went to the other world—
A hero had arisen fully equal to him.
If you ask about the boy,
His forefather Tugol Khan
Had been blessed by Khizr from the beginning.
His roots were in the line of saints.
His distant ancestor was Boyon Khan;
From Boyon Khan came Chayan Khan,
From Chayan Khan, Bala Khan.
Bala Khan's hero,
Who never drew back from what he faced,
Who never turned away from death,
Was Ogoy Khan, born a warrior.
High-browed and fierce in wrath,
He too laid much of China low.
He brought strife to many places,
Broke royal courts and took spoils,
Saw deserts where no soul traveled,
Roamed the world and saw its lands.
He traveled along the rivers.
Before impetuous Ogoy,
Those who faced him crawled.
Renowned Ogoy rose as khan;
His voice drove the life from men.
He had been lowly at the hearth,
And grew mighty through sucking blood.
With that dear Ogoy Khan,
Those who clashed were brought low.
From Ogoy Khan came Kara Khan;
From ill-intentioned Zhakyp,
From the dark, gray-maned hero,
From renowned gray-maned Manas,
Semetey was born with sacred might.
Zhylgynduu and Talas became his land;
A hero named Semetey arose.
Before, to Temir Khan's city
He had wandered and suffered humiliation.
Semetey found his lineage,
Came to Talas and grew mighty,
And among the Argyn and Kyrgyz
Stood as a fortress.
Of the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
Those left alive after the deaths said:
“Semetey has become sultan;
He has settled once more upon his seat.
The thin horses have grown fat,
The hungry bellies have been filled.
Now things have turned out well.”
He made Talas his homeland,
Gathered the scattered into a people,
Made the grieving folk a people.
To the poor who came without livestock,
He allotted shares and made them wealthy,
And thus set their hearts at ease.
Maintaining a royal court, a khan,
He became a man securely established.
His anxious heart relaxed,
His troubled sorrow healed,
All the villains vanished.
The bold son of Manas
Had come to live in this way.
Like a deep-rooted, towering willow,
Semetey had come from Bukhara,
And over the Argyn and Kyrgyz
Become governor, sultan and khan.
Taking the boy as their protector,
They had settled there.
Spirits by day, meat by night—
That was how things had become.
All of the Kyrgyz,
The young and the old,
Drank kumis and courted girls,
In many games and entertainments
They were immersed.
Racing horses, playing ordo,
In entertainments such as these
They were immersed.
Riding horses in their third year, flying hawks,
They played in wild delight.
An entire otter pelt
They split in two,
And trimmed their trouser legs with it.
At Zhylgynduu, Ken-Kol and broad Talas
They settled in bustling throngs.
Even those calling themselves the poorest
Tethered a thousand foals apiece.
Thus increasing their splendor,
From pale, fresh kumis
They had spirits distilled in streams.
Such were the Kyrgyz people's pleasures.
Now let us tell another tale:
Semetey and Chynkozho,
And the bitter quarrel that arose!
On Friday's sacred Night of Power,
In Semetey's royal court
Was his aged uncle Bakai.
Along Uch-Koshoi,
The Argyn khan, Sary Khan,
Was there too, to offer counsel.
His mother Kanykei—
A saint in a white headscarf—
His unfortunate mother Kanykei was there.
All the wise khans were there.
Bringing his forty treasury guards,
An inheritance left by Manas,
Who had stirred the stars in heaven,
Who had been a friend of David,
A man of sacred power,
A khan of treasures,
The smith Bolokbai was there too.
Tekechi's Ormonbek—
When all the khans had gathered,
The bold son born of Manas
Had these words to say:
“Almambet's son Kulchoro,
My kinsman like a twin lamb,
Has reached twelve years of age.
For this very one's wish
I have prayed to God.
My flag fixed upon a spear,
My father's friend Almambet
Saying, “Let him take him as support,”
Left as a gift for me.
This Kulchoro standing here—
That his heart might be fat,
I had a young mare slaughtered,
And fed him his fill of its belly fat.
When he was six, I took him,
Had an amulet hung about his neck,
And among the Argyn and Kyrgyz
Had him raised with loving care.
I let him wear no dirty shirt,
Nor drink from a dirty bowl.
I took the child as my protector,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro
I had suckled in equal shares.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
My poplars set before me for protection,
From Almambet and Chubak
The charge I inherited.
My protective otter at my collar,
The bright star above your head.
Kicking one another like young colts,
‘Let their name be something special,’
My sorrowful mother Kanykei said.
To make them true kin,
She suckled them with milk from her white breasts.
They shared the same delights;
Semetey and these boys
Lay upon one bed.
Our blood is one, our souls separate.
Impartial khans, hear me!
Kulchoro is twelve,
Kanchoro is fourteen.
These are noble at their roots,
Children of princes.
Semetey, his father's only son,
Has taken these two as his support.
At sight of them my longing is eased.
If hardship falls upon my troubled head,
Through whom I shall inflict grievous torment.
Khans gathered in your ranks, hear me:
My tail feathers have matured.
When its wings have grown to match,
Would a falcon stand unready?
God has understood my wish.
When the days are counted,
When the days are set in writing,
The weapon at my side,
This Kulchoro standing here,
Has reached twelve years this year.
My Kanchoro, whom I take as support,
Has reached fourteen years.
With leopard Bakai at your head,
Impartial khans, look here!
Can a prince's son,
Without seeking news of the Chinese,
Simply stand and watch?
A nobleman's only son—
Can he lie without a care,
Once his stride has reached its strength,
Without breaking ranks in spear combat,
Without falling to a bullet if his time has come,
In paradisal Great Beijing
Without fighting in the tumult?
Can one become a man without doing so?
One of the seven days is death;
Can one who fears death prosper?
The Chinese with their sovereign, the khagan's people—
Can we refrain from fighting them?
With the Chin khagan and Machin,
Can a man remain without a quarrel?
If we simply lie in one place,
Will God not strike us down?
Dark as a cloud of mist,
With my father Khan Manas at their head,
Against the true Chinese in Beijing,
May we die if we do not fight!
‘I was born of a father as a man’—
Better that we had never been born!
This year against the mottled-bearded Manchu
Let us openly wage a holy war.
Against the unbelievers like black worms,
Let us charge with level spears!
The Argyn and Kyrgyz are brothers.
Shygai's son Chynkozho
Let us fasten at our waist as support.
If Chynkozho agrees to my plan,
I shall gird my waist firmly.
From Kongurbai in Beijing
I shall exact my father's blood-price.
